newsitem.title: UK: British January retail prices key to interest rates.
newsitem.headline: British January retail prices key to interest rates.

text.p: Underlying British inflation should have eased in January as seasonal sales discounts took the sting out of high street prices, analysts said on Tuesday.
January's retail price numbers are due at 0930 GMT on Thursday.
The Reuters consensus forecast is for the annual rate of underlying inflation (RPIX), which excludes mortgages interest payments, to have dipped to 3.0 percent last month from 3.1 in December.
But the headline rate is seen rising to 2.7 percent from 2.5 previously.

Analysts said the January numbers will be pushed and pulled by a mixture of factors, and there is a risk that both headline and underlying rates may have ticked higher. Either way, the move is likely to be small.
The key to victory in the interest rate battle between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George will lie in specific components of the price index.

With the downward pressure of January sales pitted against potential upward pressure from annual price rises, a cold winter and higher mortgage rates, some analysts say Clarke, who is keen not to tighten rates before the next election, may come across some problems.

"My suspicion is that underlying inflation will increase, and there is a good chance that the headline rate will increase even if the underlying doesn't," said Glenn Davies, chief UK economist at Credit Lyonnais in London.
He said the increase in mortgage rates sparked by a 0.25 percent rise in base rates on October 30 last year was now feeding through.
Neil Parker at Royal Bank of Scotland said the mortgage rate effect would be heightened by the fact that last year's late increase contrasted with a cut in rates the year before.
"We expect headline inflation to fall by 0.1 percent on the month, with the year-on-year rate ticking up slightly to 2.7 percent," Parker said.
With the Bank of England's inflation report due on Wednesday, the key to whether Thursday's data will back Clarke or George rests on whether seasonal or non-seasonal factors dominate the RPI index.
George and Clarke have disagreed on interest rates since December last year, when George's call for a further 0.25 percent rise in rates was ignored.

Lehman Brothers economist Michael Dicks said the small rise in mortgage rates will block any fall in headline inflation, but the overall picture would present no threat to Clarke's desire to hold base rates at 6.0 percent.
Parker at RBS said while January sale discounts would exert some downward pressure, he did not expect it to have been as aggressive as in January 1996.

A report overnight from the British Retail Consortium said retail sales edged up in January, driven mainly by price gains in non-food sector. It showed an annual increase of 4.9 percent in the year-on-yaer value of retail sales in January, up from 4.3 percent in December.
But BRC chief economic adviser Andrew Sentance said retail spending was not growing strongly enough to constitute an inflationary danger.
